turn1.explanation: The unit fires on sentence- and clause-boundary punctuation (commas, periods, semicolons) in documents whose earlier context mentions ships, boats or other vessels. It responds more weakly when the earlier context contains only a nautical-adjacent word such as 'anchor' (a company name or SEO 'anchor text') or 'vessels' in another sense (blood vessels), or when it is just long running prose.
turn1.evidence: The strongest values (3.5–4.2) fall on ',' and '.' in boat and ship texts: SeaArk boats, powerships/power barges, a cruise-ship casino, the Swedish ship listing, flying boats and V.Ships crew. Weaker examples have looser maritime cues: anchor-electronics.com (~3), Google 'anchor' text (~3), the Stargate ship (~2.5), the CT scan with 'vessels' (~1.7), and the cargo ship or rig wreckage texts (~1.2). The content words themselves stay near zero (e.g. 'boat' 0.13, 'Jamaica' 0.15).
turn1.missing_data: Punctuation-dense documents with no ship or anchor context at all, to tell a maritime-context gate apart from generic punctuation in list-heavy prose. The TV/radio news example, at ~2.5, has only a weak link to vessels and is the main counterexample.
